items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: Now we have, in this band, Robinson, Stillworth, Shields, Bara, Christian, and myself.

ctx.x: Go right ahead. You played the show.

We played the show. Before we played the show, we rehearsed in the show. When all the Englishmen laughed at us, the papers carried reports that we was a dog band. Some of them said we was yelping hounds. And they didn't describe our music with anything but was no good. That's the critics in London. And you have a picture that was taken backstage. And all the people sitting down are reporters. That afternoon on the 5th, we opened in the show. We got a fair hand for when the doughboys from the United States Army…
The man offered me jobs to come back. I had jobs for Paris. And I came back to New York in 1920. I left English piano player. Can we stop now? Yeah.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1960-01-03
items.q: So I played the melody, and like I say, Shields put the lace on it, and the trombone players sewed it up

ctx.x: That's right, they're credited with authorship. Now, will you tell me this, Nick, is there any story behind the satanic blues? In other words, these fellas didn't read too much music either. Did they take this, or did they just act a composer?

They'll give me an idea of how, why don't you make a tune on this? Well, it was a cooperative band, and it didn't make no difference whose name went on the tunes. So I played the melody, and like I say, Shields put the lace on it, and the trombone players sewed it up, whether he was Edwards or Christian, they sewed it up, and that was the way I started playing.
Well, before we play this record, let me just ask you one thing, Nick. There's been a lot of misunderstanding. The original Dixieland jazz band was composed of good friends. Isn't this so?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: We had Shields, myself, Spobara, Edwards and what's his name?

ctx.x: I hate to interrupt you on that story but I missed out a couple of things. I didn't get who was in the band at the time. I know Edwards was back. He replaced Christian and I didn't get the names of the other bands.

Now I'll tell you the names of the men. Robertson joined us as piano player which he had been the first steady piano player after Regis' death. We had Shields, myself, Spobara, Edwards and what's his name? Roberts had made the five of us.
And that's immediately upon coming back from London. That's right. Robertson Hilton. And then what was the name of the saxophone players? I want to get that to you.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: And in November, Shields was playing with me again. He had played with me in New Orleans before he left there.

ctx.x: I'll write you again soon. I wish to you and your family a very good Happy New Year. And Holly Expus, your friend J.C. Avoté, and he signs it Jean C. Avoté. P.S. You will find in this letter the results of my investigations in the New York newspapers between 1915 and 1919. What he means about his typewriter is that he wrote the E key and he has to put acute marks and grave marks on his E's. It's the only way he can finish a letter.

Well, he wrote down to Mr. Howard Jacobs. He put a piece in the paper for asking for an old time jazz band to write him. That he was trying to clear up the great mystery that hangs over the jazz. That someone should get credit where it should be. Now many people ask, amongst this one was this Tom Brown and the record changer. Well, now these things I had never known before, the record changer, the claims that Brown made. These had just come to my mind. Now when you have a family to support you, just don't jump up…

It says, uh, CCE, DJ LaRocca, number 2218 Constant Street. October the 14th, 1957, I see. Heading of the letter, Mr. Harry V. Sushant, comma, President, New Orleans Jazz Club, comma, 2417 Octavia Street, New Orleans, Louisiana. Dear Harry, colon, for many months now, comma, I have delayed writing you concerning a matter, a matter, that I know means a great deal to you and the members of your organization, period. This matter means a great deal to me, comma, personally, comma, because one of the principal…
